analysis.one_liner: Blocks all new federal, state, and local cryptocurrency regulation for five years and defers taxes on crypto income until it is converted to dollars.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced and died there when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have banned federal, state, and local governments from passing any new rules specifically about cryptocurrency for five years starting June 1, 2015. It also would have told the IRS to stop treating cryptocurrency as property—where gains are taxed each time it's used—and instead tax it like currency, collecting tax only when someone converts crypto into dollars. Existing criminal and tax laws could still be enforced, but no new ones could be written during the moratorium.
analysis.who_benefits: Cryptocurrency holders, miners, and would-be exchanges would gain the most: five years free of any new federal, state, or local crypto rules, and a tax bill due only when coins are converted to dollars rather than every time they're spent. People who used crypto for everyday purchases would avoid the paperwork of tracking gains on each transaction under the IRS's property treatment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Early crypto holders, miners, and exchanges

how_it_helps.text: It would bar federal, state, and local governments from imposing any new statute or regulation specifically governing the creation, use, possession, or transfer of cryptocurrency for five years, shielding the young industry from new rules.

It would direct the IRS to treat cryptocurrency as currency rather than property, and to tax income from crypto received in business, or mined, only when it is converted into dollars—so holders pay no tax on gains until they cash out.
It declares the IRS's existing guidance (Notice 2014-21), which taxes crypto as property at fair market value, to be 'less than optimal' and orders interim regulations to replace it.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers at large would bear the cost of deferred tax collection on crypto gains, and consumers would bear the risk of a market left without new fraud or safety rules for five years, since the moratorium applies to state and local governments too.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and consumers facing unregulated crypto

drawbacks.text: A five-year ban on new cryptocurrency rules would have left consumers without updated protections in a market already prone to exchange failures, theft, and fraud, since Section 2(b) only preserved enforcement of laws already on the books, not new rules for new schemes.

The tax deferral provisions would have delayed federal revenue: income from crypto received in business or from mining would be taxed only when converted to dollars, pushing collections into the future and complicating enforcement.

The bill was legally awkward: it purported to suspend enactment and effectiveness of pending state and federal statutes and regulations, a sweeping preemption of state authority that courts would likely have tested under the severability clause the bill itself included.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For its intended beneficiaries—early cryptocurrency holders, miners, and would-be exchanges—the bill was a clear win: five years with no new rules and taxes due only when coins were converted to dollars. For everyone else the costs outweighed that: state and federal governments would have been barred from writing consumer-protection rules in a market already notorious for hacks and fraud, federal and state treasuries would have collected tax later or not at all, and the IRS would have been directed to rewrite its guidance to suit one industry. The bill also showed little sign of workable design—it never advanced far enough for hearings or committee scrutiny, and it attracted no cosponsors even among members generally sympathetic to reducing regulation.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, neither ever took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced December 1, 2014, with no cosponsors, and referred the same day to the House Financial Services and Ways and Means Committees.
The only actions ever taken on the bill were introduction and referral; neither committee held a hearing, marked it up, or reported it out.
The 113th Congress ended January 3, 2015, and all bills not passed by both chambers die when a Congress ends.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and taxpayers: cryptocurrency stayed subject to existing law, including the IRS's property tax treatment.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers and tax enforcement kept existing rules

for.name: Rep. Steve Stockman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 1, 2014, in the final weeks of the 113th Congress.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died in committee without any action after referral.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and never reached a vote, so no partisan split was ever measured.

industries.industry: Cryptocurrency holders, miners, and early exchanges
industries.note: A five-year ban on new crypto regulation plus tax deferral until coins are converted to dollars would have let early adopters grow holdings tax-free and operate free of new federal, state, or local rules. The main beneficiaries would be the small group of people already holding or mining coins and the businesses hoping to trade them.

The bill would have stripped states and localities of the power to pass any new rules specifically governing cryptocurrency for five years, blocking them from protecting residents against fraud or loss in a fast-moving market.
